mcqs.question: Three worker processes all listen on the same point-to-point queue of "resize image" jobs. How many workers process a single given job?
options: All three, in parallel, to be safe
Exactly one — the queue delivers each message to a single consumer even with multiple listeners
Zero, until a fourth worker joins the pool
It depends on the size of the image being resized
mcqs.explanation: Point-to-point delivery guarantees exactly one consumer handles each message, which is what makes competing consumers safe for work that must happen once. Having all three process it would double- or triple-charge the work; the image size doesn't change the delivery guarantee.

mcqs.question: An "order placed" event needs to reach an email service, a fraud-check service, and an analytics pipeline, each independently. Which pattern fits?
options: A point-to-point queue with three competing consumers
A single synchronous API call chained through all three services in sequence
Pub/sub — each service subscribes and gets its own copy of the event
A shared database table that each service polls in turn
mcqs.explanation: All three services need to react to the same event independently, not share one unit of work, which is exactly what pub/sub is for. A competing-consumers queue would only let one of them see any given message, and a chained synchronous call couples all three services' uptime together unnecessarily.

mcqs.question: Under a load spike, a team adds a fourth worker process to a pool reading from a busy point-to-point queue. What does the competing-consumers pattern give them for free?
options: Automatic message deduplication across all four workers
Guaranteed processing order across the four workers
A rebalance step the broker must run before the new worker can help
The broker starts routing messages to the new worker immediately, spreading load without any coordination code
mcqs.explanation: New workers just start pulling from the queue as soon as they connect — no coordination or rebalance step needed, which is the whole appeal of competing consumers. It doesn't provide deduplication or cross-worker ordering guarantees on its own.

mcqs.question: You're deciding between a queue and pub/sub for a new event type. What's the single question that should decide it?
options: If I add a second listener, do I want it to share the existing work or get its own full copy of every message?
Which one has lower network latency in general?
Which one is faster to set up initially?
Which broker product does the team already have a license for?
mcqs.explanation: That question directly maps to the two delivery models: sharing work means a queue, getting a full independent copy means pub/sub. Latency, setup speed, and licensing might influence which product you pick, but they don't determine which delivery pattern the message actually needs.

mcqs.question: The shipping team only wants order events tagged "orders.confirmed," while payments only wants "orders.payment-failed." What's the right mechanism?
options: Have every subscriber receive the full stream and filter client-side
Topics or routing keys, so each subscriber only receives the slice tagged relevant to it
Split the publisher into three separate publishers, one per interested team
Switch from pub/sub to a point-to-point queue
mcqs.explanation: Routing keys or topics let the broker do the filtering, so each subscriber only receives what it asked for, without extra publishers or client-side filtering overhead. Switching to a queue would break the fan-out both teams still need.
